opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that the two complement each other more than they compete.

For a lot of what people want to do with Nano Banana, in-context examples go surprisingly far. Because the model is built on top of a strong multimodal language model, it's quite good at looking at a few reference images, a character, a product, a particular style, and carrying that through into new generations or edits. That's really the magic for most users. You don't want to collect a dataset and run a training job just to keep your dog looking like your dog across five images. You want to show it a picture and say "put him on a skateboard." So a lot of our effort has gone into making the model a really good in-context learner: consistency, following references, understanding what you actually meant from the examples you gave.

That said, I don't think fine-tuning goes away. There are cases where you have a very specific visual language, say a brand with strict guidelines, or a specialized domain like a certain kind of technical illustration, where you need that behavior to be reliable across thousands of generations, and stuffing examples into every prompt gets expensive or still doesn't capture all the subtlety. There, adapting the weights still makes sense.

The way I think about it is that the better the base model's in-context abilities get, the higher the bar for when you actually need to fine-tune. A couple of years ago you basically had to fine-tune, with DreamBooth-style approaches, to get any kind of subject consistency. Now that's often a zero-shot or few-shot capability. So fine-tuning shifts toward the long tail: really specialized, high-volume, high-precision use cases. And honestly, as a researcher, that's the direction I want things to go, because in-context is so much more accessible. Anyone can do it just by talking to the model.

r001.rationale: The response compares in-context examples with fine-tuning, but does not draw the specified analogy to language models or say that putting fine-tuning examples in context can substitute for fine-tuning.

r002.rationale: It says fine-tuning makes sense for cases such as strict brand guidelines and specialized domains requiring reliable behavior across many generations, describing these as high-volume, high-precision uses.

r003.rationale: It says in-context examples go far for many user needs and expresses a preference for that approach becoming more accessible, which communicates hope that examples in context will serve most use cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something we think about a lot. I'd say my honest view is that for most of what people want to do with Nano Banana, in-context examples are winning, and they're winning more every generation.

The thing that changed is that these models are now natively multimodal in a pretty deep way. So when you give Nano Banana a reference image and say "put this character in this scene" or "match this lighting," it's not going through some retrieval pipeline or a bolted-on adapter. The image is just tokens in the context, same as the text, and the model reasons over them together. That means consistency, style transfer, character identity, all the things that used to require a LoRA or a DreamBooth-style fine-tune, you can increasingly just show the model and it gets it. That's a huge quality-of-life shift for users, because fine-tuning was always this awkward thing where you'd spend an hour collecting data and training, and then your subject still looked slightly off.

Where I think fine-tuning still earns its place is in a few spots. One is when you have a very specific distribution that's genuinely out of the model's experience, like a proprietary product catalog with thousands of SKUs, or a very particular brand aesthetic you need to hit at scale, every time, without supervision. Another is cost and latency. If you're running millions of generations with the same reference, stuffing those references into context on every call adds up, and baking that knowledge into weights can be the more efficient path. And the third is the long tail of weird domains, medical imagery, satellite data, things where the base prior just isn't rich enough to be steered by a couple of examples.

But I'd frame it almost like how it played out with language models. A few years ago everyone was fine-tuning for everything, and now most teams reach for prompting and in-context examples first, and fine-tuning is the thing you do when you've measured that you actually need it. I think image models are on that same trajectory, just a couple of years behind. Our goal with Nano Banana is really to push the in-context side as far as we can, because that's the version that puts the capability in everyone's hands rather than just the people with a training pipeline.

r001.rationale: The response compares image models to language models, where teams now try prompting and in-context examples first and fine-tune only when needed.

r002.rationale: It identifies specific cases where fine-tuning may help, such as proprietary catalogs or high-volume generation, but does not predict that professional uses of Nano Banana generally will benefit from it.

r003.rationale: It says in-context examples are winning for most things people want to do with Nano Banana and expresses a goal of pushing that approach further.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful distinction is whether you’re trying to guide a particular request or establish behavior you want consistently across many requests. In-context examples let you show the model what you mean without changing its weights, so they’re a natural place to start when you’re still exploring the task.

Fine-tuning becomes interesting when you have a stable requirement and examples alone aren’t giving you the consistency you need. But I wouldn’t make a strong claim about that tradeoff for Nano Banana without a direct comparison. I’d start with examples, look at where they fail, and use those failures to decide whether fine-tuning is worth pursuing.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame it as a question of what you need to persist. In-context examples let you show the model what you want for a particular task, and they’re easy to change as you iterate. Fine-tuning makes more sense when you have a consistent behavior you want across many requests and a good set of examples to train on.

For Nano Banana, I’d start with in-context examples and see where they fall short. If you keep supplying the same guidance and still see recurring failures, that’s a reason to explore fine-tuning—assuming it’s available. But I wouldn’t assume fine-tuning is automatically better; I’d compare the two on the specific behavior you care about.
